# Introduction {#sec-intro}

The previous study -- [Portfolio Optimization](https://konilo.github.io/sandbox/sandbox/portfolio_optimization/portfolio_optimization.html) -- set out to design a portfolio optimized for utility maximization which requires solving @eq-challenge.

$$
\underbrace{\frac{\text{return}}{\text{risk}}}_{\text{to maximize}} \times \underbrace{\text{leverage}}_{\substack{\text{to adapt to my} \\ \text{risk aversion level}}}
$$ {#eq-challenge}

The tool used to borrow cash and lever up the portfolio is a specific combination of options called a short box spread. This is the topic of this study.

Some key facts about short box spreads:

- they act as fixed-rate loans: get $x$ today and pay back $y$ on a given date, with $x$, $y$, and the term date being known from the start and fixed, and $x < y$;
    https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_spread
    https://www.investopedia.com/terms/b/boxspread.asp
    https://earlyretirementnow.com/2021/12/09/low-cost-leverage-box-spread/
- they are accessible to French citizens (via a compte-titres ordinaire from the most sophisticated brokers such as Interactive Brokers);
    https://www.reddit.com/r/vosfinances/comments/1tqzjd4/cayas_meilleur_que_le_100_world/
    https://cayas.fr/le-journal/ouvrir-et-configurer-son-compte-interactive-brokers
- they surpass other forms of borrowing (such as consumer credit, lombard credit, leveraged ETFs) in terms of allocation constraints and rate, at the cost of additional complexity;
    https://youtu.be/fYO19-YkulI
- they require some expertise^[margin, options] and automated monitoring^[margin maintenance], which means that they are not suitable for all investors.


# Semantics

Find some fundamentals about options in Elton et al. ([2014](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/shop/general-finance-investments/modern-portfolio-theory-and-investment-analysis-9th-edition-p-9781118469941); chapter 23), for instance. The main terms used herein are defined in @tbl-semantics.

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| Being long on an option | Having bought an option and holding it |
| Being short on an option | Having sold an option (which is not yet expired or exercised), aka having written an option |
| To long a call (LC) | Buying and holding a call |
| To long a put (LP) | Buying and holding a put |
| To short a call (SC) | Writing a call (which is not yet expired or exercised) |
| To short a put (SP) | Writing a put (which is not yet expired or exercised) |
| A box spread | (LC + SP) + (SC + LP), each parens being a leg |
| Leg 1 of a box spread | LC + SP at the same strike i.e., a synthetic long forward (Gantin, [2026](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/s/synthetic-forward-contract.asp)) |
| Leg 2 of a box spread | SC + LP at the same strike i.e., a synthetic short forward (ibid.) |
| To short a box spread | Having sold a box spread, i.e., borrowing cash |
| To long box spread | Having bought a box spread i.e., lending cash |
: Semantics {#tbl-semantics}


# Understanding a short box spread
## Variables

The variables used in this deconstruction of short box spreads are defined as follows:

- $K_1$ = the strike price of the 1st leg's options
- $K_2$ = the strike price of the 2nd leg's options
- $C_1$ = the premium of leg 1's call
- $C_2$ = the premium of leg 2's call
- $P_1$ = the premium of leg 1's put
- $P_2$ = the premium of leg 2's put
- $S_E$ = the price of the underlying security at expiration

Options generally control 100 shares of the underlying security but the literature's standard doesn't include a $\times100$ factor ^[from my experience, at least]. For accuracy, the formulas herein consider options controlling a single share. This choice only affects the option premiums which are divided by 100 relative to the real ones.

Box spreads must be implemented using [European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Option_style), [cash-settled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Option_(finance)#According_to_the_delivery_type) options. This study only considers options of this type.


## The payoff of each leg of a short box spread

| Part of the leg to short | Corresponding action | Now | At expiration | Ditto |
|---|---|---|---|---|
|  |  |  | If $S_E > K_1$ | If $S_E \leq K_1$ |
| LC | Shorting a LC i.e., writing a call | $C_1$^[being paid the call's premium] | $(K_1 - S_E)$^[paying the call's intrinsic value $S_E - K_1$ in cash (as it is in the money)] | $0$^[the call expires worthless] |
| SP | Shorting a SP i.e., buying a put | $-P_1$^[paying the put's premium] | $0$^[the put expires worthless] | $(K_1 - S_E)$^[being paid the put's intrinsic value $K_1 - S_E$ in cash (as it is in the money)] |
| Total |  | $C_1-P_1$ | $(K_1 - S_E)$^[same payoff in both cases: it's a synthetic short forward (which allows one to sell the underlying security for a fixed price on a given, future date)] | $(K_1 - S_E)$ |
: Shorting leg 1 of the box spread {#tbl-leg1}

| Part of the leg to short | Corresponding action | Now | At expiration | Ditto |
|---|---|---|---|---|
|  |  |  | If $S_E > K_2$ | If $S_E \leq K_2$ |
| SC | Shorting a SC i.e., buying a call | $-C_2$^[paying the call's premium] | $(S_E - K_2)$^[being paid the call's intrinsic value $S_E - K_2$ in cash (as it is in the money)] | $0$^[the call expires worthless] |
| LP | Shorting a LP i.e., writing a put | $P_2$^[being paid the put's premium] | $0$^[the put expires worthless] | $(S_E - K_2)$^[paying the put's intrinsic value $K_2 - S_E$ in cash (as it is in the money)] |
| Total |  | $-C_2+P_2$ | $(S_E - K_2)$^[same payoff in both cases, it's a synthetic long forward (which allows one to buy the underlying security for a fixed price on a given, future date)] | $(S_E - K_2)$ |
: Shorting leg 2 of the box spread {#tbl-leg2}

While initiating a short box spread clearly consists in buying or selling calls and puts, the process to repay the resulting loan can be less intuitive and, I think, deserves some more explanations. A short box spread loan is generally repaid by letting its options be exercised or expire worthless on the expiration date. Settlement is made automatically in cash drawing from the CTO's cash^[or on margin if the cash balance is too low, which should be prevented by rolling the options earlier; more on that further down]. (Early repayment is also possible by going long on the same 4 options which cancels out the 8 options. It implies some rate risk, bid/ask spread costs, and trading fees.)

## Solving the cashflows

| Leg                   | Now                     | At expiration |
| --------------------- | ----------------------- | ------------- |
| 1: shorting (LC + SP) | $C_1-P_1$               | $(K_1 - S_E)$ |
| 2: shorting (SC + LP) | $-C_2+P_2 = -(C_2-P_2)$ | $(S_E - K_2)$ |
| Total                 | $C_1-P_1-(C_2-P_2)$     | $(K_1 - K_2)$ |
: Cashflows {#tbl-together}

The cashflow at expiration is now solved. But the cashflow "Now" is not, yet.

In liquid markets, [put-call parity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Put%E2%80%93call_parity) Elton et al. ([2014](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/shop/general-finance-investments/modern-portfolio-theory-and-investment-analysis-9th-edition-p-9781118469941); chapter 23) teaches us that $$C = S_0 + P - \frac{K}{1+R}$$ where

- $S_0$ = the stock price now (1 share)
- $K$ = the strike price
- assuming $R_L = R_B = R$. But apparently it's false. TODO.

Hence $$C - P = S_0 - \frac{K}{1+R}$$
Applying that to leg 1: $$C_1 - P_1 = S_0 - \frac{K_1}{1+R}$$
And to leg 2: $$C_2 - P_2 = S_0 - \frac{K_2}{1+R}$$
Substituting in the expression of the cashflow "Now" from the table above:
$\text{new cashflow} = $C_1-P_1-(C_2-P_2)$$
$$S_0 - \frac{K_1}{1+R} - \big(S_0 - \frac{K_2}{1+R}\big)$$
$$S_0 - \frac{K_1}{1+R} - S_0 + \frac{K_2}{1+R}$$
$$-\frac{K_1}{1+R} + \frac{K_2}{1+R}$$
$$\frac{-K_1 + K_2}{1+R} = \frac{K_2-K_1}{1+R}$$


## Putting it together

Scaling back to the realistic 100-share-controlling options and assuming the legs are built such that $K_1 < K_2$, shorting a box spread:

- initially provides $$\frac{100(K_2-K_1)}{1+R}$$; that's the present value of the difference between the two strikes, using the borrowing rate;
- and costs $$100(K_1 - K_2)$$ at expiration; that's the (negative) difference between the two strikes.

Receive a given amount today, and pay back more, eventually.


# Sizing a short box spread loan

- The amount owed at expiration date (= the **face** of the loan) is $$face = 100 \times N_{boxes} \times -(K_1 - K_2)$$ ^[The added "$-$" just converts the negative cashflow expression from above into a positive amount]. It's controlled by both
	- the strike width $K_1-K_2$ of the boxe(s)
	- and the number of boxes sold $N_{boxes}$

in both cases, the higher the

- The amount obtained initially (= the loan's **principal**) is the present value of the face value $$principal=\frac{100N_{boxes}(K_2-K_1)}{1+R}$$
- The **term** of the loan is defined by the expiration date of the options of the boxes (which must be identical)
- The rate ($R$) is not under one's direct control -- it's implied and is a function of the market's risk free rate for the maturity chosen for the box (?? not yet understood, that's for later TODO). You can act on
	- the maturity/expiration date of the options
	- timing: shorting opportunistically when the market's implied rate on box spreads is favorable relative to other borrowing methods
